title: GATE Score vs Marks: How Your GATE Score Is Calculated
description: GATE score calculation, step by step: the official GATE 2027 formula that turns marks out of 100 into a score anchored at 350 and 900, the qualifying-mark rule, and a fully worked example.
author: Studyloaf Team

content.body: Your GATE scorecard shows marks out of 100 and a GATE score, and the two are different numbers. Marks are what you earned on the paper. The score places those marks on a scale shared across the whole paper, using a formula in the GATE 2027 information brochure. Here is that formula, what each part means, and a worked example.

content.heading: Step 1: marks
content.body: For a paper held in a single session, your marks are your actual marks. For a paper held in more than one session, your marks are first normalized so different sessions can be compared. That step is explained in our separate post on GATE normalization. Either way, the result is the M in the score formula.

content.heading: Step 2: the qualifying mark
content.body: For general-category candidates, the qualifying mark of a paper is max(25, min(40, μ + σ)), where μ and σ are the mean and standard deviation of the marks of everyone who appeared in that paper. It is mean plus one standard deviation, but never below 25 and never above 40. OBC-NCL and EWS candidates qualify at nine-tenths of the general mark, and SC, ST and PwD candidates at two-thirds of it.

content.heading: Step 3: the score formula
content.body: GATE Score = Sq + (St − Sq) × (M − Mq) ÷ (M̄t − Mq). Sq is 350 and St is 900. Mq is the general-category qualifying mark from step 2. M̄t is the mean marks of the top 0.1% of candidates in the paper, or of the top 10 if that is a larger group. So a candidate exactly at the qualifying mark scores 350, and a candidate exactly at the top performers' average scores 900, with everyone else placed proportionally.

content.heading: Worked example
content.body: Invented numbers for a single-session paper: μ + σ works out to 28.6, and the top performers average 78 marks. Since 28.6 lies between 25 and 40, Mq = 28.6. A general candidate with 50 marks scores 350 + 550 × (50 − 28.6) ÷ (78 − 28.6) = 350 + 550 × 21.4 ÷ 49.4 = 350 + 238.26 ≈ 588.

content.heading: The 25 and 40 limits in action
list: A hard paper where μ + σ is 22: the qualifying mark is lifted to 25
An easy paper where μ + σ is 45: the qualifying mark is capped at 40
Anywhere in between, the qualifying mark is μ + σ itself

content.heading: What this means for you
content.body: The same marks can give different scores in different papers or years, because Mq and M̄t come from that year's candidates in that paper. That's the point of the score: it measures where you stand in your paper, not raw marks. Each admitting institute decides for itself how it uses the score, and a GATE 2027 score stays valid for three years from the results date.

content.heading: Common mistakes
list: Treating the score as marks times ten. It is anchored to the qualifying mark (350) and the top performers' average (900)
Using last year's qualifying mark. It is recalculated from each year's mean and standard deviation
Comparing raw marks with a friend in another session of a multi-session paper. Only normalized marks compare
